blindSummary:
This country is comparatively safe for transgender visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 1993, discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, and SOGI was added to the hate-crime provisions of the criminal code in 2015. Legal gender recognition exists via a medicalised process, and the capital has an organised community (an LGBT community centre) that successfully lobbied for these protections.

Counterweights: protections are fragmented (no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering all areas), the community centre has documented periods of elevated hate speech and assaults — including attacks on its own staff — and social acceptance outside the capital is low. There are no bathroom laws, no border/document friction for foreign passports, and no police targeting pattern; the realistic risk is street harassment if visibly trans, particularly at night and outside the central districts of the capital.
blindOutOfScope: Comprehensive anti-discrimination gaps and the medicalised legal-gender-recognition process are resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): notable progress since decriminalisation in 1993 - discrimination based on SOGI prohibited, but no comprehensive anti-discrimination law (protections fragmented); marriage equality constitutionally prohibited; legal gender recognition possible but requires medical intervention (not self-determination); hate-crime and non-discrimination provisions exist in penal and labour codes but enforcement is inconsistent.

A country page on an international LGBTI legal-rights database: documents this country's LGBTI-related legal frameworks — status of same-sex conduct, anti-discrimination provisions and gender-recognition data.
A multilateral development bank's publication on the legal status of sexual and gender minorities across a large multi-country region - comparative overview including this country.

Online magazine (Aug 2018): profile of LGBTQ activism in one developing country - features an activist who came out three times (as a lesbian, then a trans man, then a gay trans man); LGBTQ activists leveraging the political transition to create progressive change.

Foreign broadcaster (Oct 2019): report that charges over an anti-LGBT attack hinted at changing attitudes - a far-right group lured a trans sex worker into a hotel room with a TV station, threatened her and aired the video with commentary accusing LGBT people of paedophilia; charges were brought and investigated as a hate crime - a first; 2017 law changes added hate-crime protections and police training.

A foreign government's diplomatic mission (March 2011): post on LGBT rights in the UN context - one member state's diplomatic advocacy for SOGI rights at the UN human-rights council, relevant to this country's international human-rights environment.

LGBT travel-news archive report on this country: homosexuality has 'virtually no presence, no venues and no activism'; no laws specifically against homosexuality but 'satisfaction of immoral sexual needs' may still be illegal; a 2008 report described two organisations holding monthly parties for hundreds of members, 'all very furtive'.
blindLocalsOnly: The medicalised legal-gender-recognition process and the fragmented anti-discrimination protections are resident-facing; the community-centre assault documentation describes residents' experience.
